title: Whoever sees us should tell himself
intro: In the account al-Mu'aybid quotes from the Book of Songs, Adi ibn Zayd and King al-Nu'man pass some graves. Adi asks the king what the graves are saying and gives them a voice. Al-Mubarrad tells the story with a tree speaking from the shade where the king has stopped. The voice recalls travellers who once drank there, then invites the listener to see himself in their place.

translation: Whoever sees us should tell himself
that he too stands on the brink of passing away.
1.sharh: The graves speak in the first person. The visitor is already poised at an edge like the tip of a spear, with very little distance left to travel.

translation: even solid mountains give way to what it brings.
2.sharh: The sentence holds back its subject, the solid mass of the mountains, until the end. Even that mass cannot outlast what time brings against it.

translation: Many a band of riders made their camels kneel beside us
and drank wine mixed with clear, cool water.
3.sharh: The verbs turn a graveyard into a stopping place again. Camels have been made to kneel and there is time to dilute the wine and sit together.

translation: The pitchers had strainers over their mouths,
and thoroughbred horses trotted about in their cloths.
4.sharh: A filter on each jug and coverings on the moving horses make the vanished party visible down to its equipment.

translation: They spent their days in a good life,
secure in their time and in no hurry.
5.sharh: The travellers felt they owned all the time ahead of them. Their unhurried pace leaves the sudden turn in the next line to do its work.

translation: Then one day time had laid them low,
as time brings down even mountains.
6.sharh: One morning is enough to change the whole scene. Mountains return from the second verse as a measure of how completely the riders have lost their strength.

translation: So time tosses a man about
from state to state as he seeks his living.
7.sharh: The man has a purpose of his own, the pursuit of a livelihood. Time is the other actor in the sentence and can throw him into circumstances he never sought.

1.2.4-5.head: قَرن زَوال
1.2.4-5.meaning: “The point of passing away.” The editor compares it to the tip of a blade.

2.2.4.head: أَصَمّ
2.2.4.meaning: Solid and compact, said here of mountains.

3.1.4.head: أَناخَ
3.1.4.meaning: Made their camels kneel so that they could dismount.

3.2.4.head: الزُّلال
3.2.4.meaning: Fresh, limpid water that goes down easily.

4.1.3.head: فِدام
4.1.3.meaning: Fidam, a straining cloth laid over the mouth of a pitcher.

4.2.3.head: رَدى
4.2.3.meaning: Trot or canter with a lifting movement.

4.2.5.head: جُلّ
4.2.5.meaning: Horsecloths draped over the backs of the animals.

5.1.1.head: عَمِرَ
5.1.1.meaning: Lived or passed their days. The diwan reads “for a time” and records the reciter’s definite form in its apparatus.

5.2.1.head: آمِن
5.2.1.meaning: Feeling secure about the time they lived in.

6.1.3.head: أَخنَعَ
6.1.3.meaning: Brought them low, made them submit.

7.2.2.head: طِلاب
7.2.2.meaning: The pursuit of something, here the search for a living.
